info.text: Lesson 03 quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: What is a variable?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Think of a labelled box: the label is the name, the box has a type (what kind of thing fits inside), and its content can be replaced later.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: A named place in memory that stores a value which can change
A fixed number that can never change
A line of text that the compiler ignores
A command that prints on the screen

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int x = 5;
x = x + 2;
cout << x << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The right side x + 2 is calculated first using the old value (5 + 2 = 7). Then 7 is stored back into x, replacing the 5.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which declaration is the best choice for storing a price such as 19.99?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Prices have a decimal part, so we need a floating-point type such as double. The other types would cut the value or turn it into something meaningless.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int p = 19.99;
cout << p << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. An int cannot hold a fraction. C++ does not round: it simply chops off the decimal part (this is called truncation), so 19.99 becomes 19.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so that each variable is declared before it is used. The program must print 7.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A variable has to exist before you read it. Here every line depends on the one above: a = 2, then b = 6, then c = 7.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int a = 2;
int b = a * 3;
int c = b + 1;
cout << c << endl;

name.text: Q06 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the best-fitting type into each gap.

main.cpp
[[1]] students = 28;
[[2]] price = 4.5;
[[3]] grade = 'A';
[[4]] passed = true;
cout << students << " " << price << " " << grade << " " << passed << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A count of students is a whole number (int), a price has decimals (double), one letter is a char, and a yes/no value is a bool.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int students = 28;
double price = 4.5;
char grade = 'A';
bool passed = true;
cout << students << " " << price << " " << grade << " " << passed << endl;

questiontext.text: What does the variable hold right after int x; (no value given) inside main?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Local variables are not cleaned automatically. Reading x before giving it a value gives garbage, so always initialize: int x = 0;.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Nothing: it is a compile error

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
cout << 7 / 2 << " " << 7 % 2 << " " << 7.0 / 2 << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Two integers divide as integers: 7 / 2 is 3 (the fraction is dropped), and % gives the remainder 1. As soon as one operand is a double (7.0) the result keeps its decimal part: 3.5.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which type should you use to store the number 5,000,000,000 (five billion)?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A typical int holds up to about 2.1 billion, so five billion would not fit. long long is large enough for numbers up to roughly 9 quintillion.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
char c = 'A';
c = c + 1;
cout << c << " " << static_cast<int>('A') << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A char is stored as a small number (the code of the letter). Adding 1 moves from 'A' to 'B', and static_cast<int>('A') reveals the stored code of 'A', which is 65.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each type with a value that fits it.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

int  →  [[1]]

double  →  [[2]]

char  →  [[3]]

bool  →  [[4]]

string  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Single quotes make one character, double quotes make text, and a number with a decimal point is a double.

The correct answer:

  • int → 42
  • double → 3.14
  • char → 'Z'
  • bool → true
  • string → "hello"

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
bool ok = (5 > 3);
bool no = (2 > 9);
cout << ok << no << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A bool is printed as a number: true becomes 1 and false becomes 0. Nothing separates them, so the output is 10.

questiontext.text:
Sort the names: can each one be used as a variable name in C++?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

score  →  [[1]]

my_score  →  [[1]]

_total  →  [[1]]

2fast  →  [[2]]

my score  →  [[2]]

class  →  [[2]]

my-score  →  [[2]]

Score2  →  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, cannot contain spaces or minus signs, and cannot be a keyword such as class. Every name here was tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Valid name: score, my_score, _total, Score2
Invalid name: 2fast, my score, class, my-score

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int a = 4;
int b = a;
a = 10;
cout << a << " " << b << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. int b = a; copies the value 4 into b once. Changing a later does not affect b: variables are separate boxes.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which of these lines is an initialization (a declaration that also gives the first value)?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. int age; only declares. age = 14; is an assignment to an existing variable. int age = 14; does both at once, which is the safest habit.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Sort each statement: is it a declaration only, an initialization, or an assignment?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

int a;  →  [[1]]

double b;  →  [[1]]

int c = 5;  →  [[2]]

char d = 'x';  →  [[2]]

a = 9;  →  [[3]]

b = 2.5;  →  [[3]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A statement that starts with a type creates a variable. If it has = value it also initializes it. A statement without a type just changes a variable that already exists.

The correct answer:

Declaration only: int a;, double b;
Initialization: int c = 5;, char d = 'x';
Assignment: a = 9;, b = 2.5;

name.text: Q17 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Complete the code so it prints the exact average 3.5 (not 3).

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
int sum = 7;
int count = 2;
double avg = static_cast<[[1]]>(sum) [[2]] count;
cout << avg << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Converting sum to double before dividing makes the division use decimals, so 7 / 2 gives 3.5. With int the fraction would be lost.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int sum = 7;
int count = 2;
double avg = static_cast<double>(sum) / count;
cout << avg << endl;

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines to calculate a discounted price. The program must print 15.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. First the price exists, then the discount is computed from it (20 / 4 = 5), then the final price (20 - 5 = 15), and only then can we print it.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int price = 20;
int discount = price / 4;
int finalPrice = price - discount;
cout << finalPrice << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
double d = 0.1 + 0.2;
cout << (d == 0.3) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Computers store decimals in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004, which is not exactly equal to 0.3. The comparison is false, printed as 0. Never compare doubles with ==.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with the type of its result.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

7 + 8  →  [[1]]

7 / 2.0  →  [[2]]

'q'  →  [[3]]

7 > 8  →  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The type of a result depends on the operands: two integers give an int, a decimal number makes it double, quotes make a char, and a comparison gives a bool.

The correct answer:

  • 7 + 8 → int
  • 7 / 2.0 → double
  • 'q' → char
  • 7 > 8 → bool
